When Everyday Responsibilities Require Twice the Effort

Perhaps you work twice as hard as everyone around you just to stay on top of emails, deadlines, appointments, and household routines.

Maybe you start projects with genuine enthusiasm, only to lose momentum halfway through, or find yourself unable to begin a task until the pressure of a last-minute deadline hits. Keys, phones, and important dates go missing. Conversations drift mid-sentence, or small frustrations trigger intense overwhelm.

For many adults, these patterns have been present for years, often masked by perfectionism, overworking, or being told you are "disorganised", "inconsistent", or "not reaching your potential".

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in adulthood can influence far more than concentration. It can shape executive functioning, time awareness, emotional regulation, energy levels, self-esteem, and relationships.

If these experiences feel familiar, you do not have to work out the next step on your own.

A clinically informed assessment and tailored psychological support can help you understand how your brain works and build practical systems that fit your everyday life.

Could This Be What You're Experiencing?

Adult ADHD can look very different from one person to another. Some adults notice persistent restlessness or impulsivity, while others primarily experience quiet internal overwhelm, mental fatigue, and difficulty organising everyday life.

You may notice that you:

  • struggle to sustain focus during meetings, reading, or routine administrative tasks
  • find it difficult to start tasks, prioritise responsibilities, or follow through to completion
  • frequently underestimate how long tasks will take or lose track of time
  • regularly misplace everyday items, forget appointments, or overlook details
  • feel mentally restless, overwhelmed by racing thoughts, or unable to switch off
  • experience strong emotional reactions, frustration, or sensitivity to criticism
  • interrupt others, speak before thinking, or make impulsive decisions
  • oscillate between intense hyperfocus on engaging tasks and mental paralysis on routine ones
  • feel chronically exhausted from trying to mask difficulties or keep up with daily demands

Experiencing these challenges does not automatically mean you have ADHD. Similar difficulties can occur alongside anxiety, depression, chronic stress, burnout, sleep disorders, trauma, or other health factors.

A comprehensive, clinically informed assessment helps clarify what may be contributing to your experiences and what type of support pathway may be appropriate.

You May Be Looking for Support Because...

Every adult reaches out for assessment or therapy at a different stage.

You may be seeking support because:

  • work, university, or parenting demands have exceeded the coping strategies you relied on earlier in life
  • you are wondering whether undiagnosed ADHD may explain lifelong patterns of overwhelm or disorganisation
  • a family member or child has been diagnosed with ADHD and you recognise similar traits in yourself
  • you have already received an ADHD diagnosis and want practical, ongoing psychological strategies
  • you are struggling with procrastination, burnout, time management, or emotional regulation
  • ADHD-related challenges are creating tension or misunderstandings in your relationships
  • you are unsure whether to begin with a psychological assessment, therapy, or a GP consultation

You do not need to have all the answers before reaching out.

Understanding Adult ADHD

Moving Beyond Willpower and Self-Blame

ADHD is a recognised neurodevelopmental condition that affects executive functioning, the cognitive processes responsible for planning, prioritising, initiating tasks, holding information in working memory, regulating emotions, and managing time.

For adults with ADHD, knowing what needs to be done is rarely the problem. The difficulty lies in bridging the gap between intention and action, especially when tasks feel repetitive, ambiguous, or low in immediate stimulation.

Over time, repeatedly falling short of your own expectations can lead to chronic stress, self-doubt, and burnout.

Understanding how executive functioning works helps shift the focus away from self-criticism and toward external structures and strategies designed around how you actually think and operate.

When Adult ADHD Affects Everyday Life

ADHD can influence several areas of adult life at once.

Focus and Task Initiation

Sustaining attention on routine responsibilities, or shifting smoothly from one task to another, can feel disproportionately draining without clear external structure.

Organisation and Time Management

Planning ahead, breaking large projects into steps, managing paperwork, and estimating time accurately can present ongoing daily hurdles.

Internal Restlessness and Mental Fatigue

In adulthood, hyperactivity often shows up internally, as a mind that rarely pauses, difficulty relaxing, or feeling constantly "on the go" even when physically tired.

Emotional Regulation

Quick flashes of frustration, feeling easily overwhelmed by minor setbacks, or struggling to recover after emotional stress can also be part of the adult ADHD experience.

Self-Esteem and Identity

Years of unspoken effort, missed deadlines, or feeling "behind" peers can quietly erode confidence and contribute to co-occurring anxiety or low mood.

Every adult's presentation is unique, and strengths such as creativity, problem-solving, and deep focus on meaningful interests often sit alongside these challenges.

When Adult ADHD Affects Relationships and Work

How Executive Functioning Ripples Outward

When everyday organisation, memory, and emotional regulation require constant effort, the impact often extends into your home life and career.

Partners, colleagues, or family members may misinterpret forgetfulness or distraction as a lack of care or commitment, while you may feel exhausted from trying to keep up.

Over time, this can contribute to:

  • misunderstandings or uneven mental load distribution with a partner
  • difficulty staying present during conversations or household routines
  • missed deadlines, unfinished projects, or workplace burnout
  • feeling defensive, guilty, or misunderstood in close relationships
  • avoiding social commitments or responsibilities due to overwhelm

Recognising these dynamics is not about blame: it provides a clearer foundation for practical communication and shared systems.

You Don't Have to Figure It Out Alone

Assessment and Psychological Support Tailored to You

Whether you are exploring a formal assessment or looking for practical post-diagnosis support, psychological care aims to meet you where you are.

Depending on your individual needs and goals, support may focus on:

  • conducting a structured, clinically informed adult ADHD assessment
  • clarifying whether ADHD, anxiety, burnout, or overlapping factors are contributing to your difficulties
  • building realistic, sustainable systems for organisation, planning, and time management
  • developing strategies for task initiation, prioritisation, and reducing procrastination
  • strengthening emotional regulation and stress-recovery skills
  • addressing long-standing self-criticism, perfectionism, or imposter feelings
  • improving communication and shared routines within relationships and family life

The goal is not to force you into a rigid mould, but to help you understand your profile, build on your strengths, and develop workable strategies for everyday life.

What Could Change with the Right Support?

With tailored assessment and psychological support, many adults gradually develop greater clarity and practical confidence in managing daily life.

Depending on your individual goals and circumstances, support may help you:

  • gain a clearer understanding of your cognitive strengths and executive functioning needs
  • reduce daily overwhelm through external systems rather than relying solely on willpower
  • approach work, study, and household responsibilities with steadier structure
  • recognise early signs of frustration or burnout and apply grounding strategies
  • communicate your needs more clearly with partners, family, or workplace supports
  • replace chronic self-blame with practical, compassionate self-management

Progress is individualised, and steady, realistic adjustments tend to create the most sustainable shifts over time.

Small Changes Can Make Everyday Life More Manageable

Practical Everyday Strategies for Adults

Adults with ADHD often benefit from externalising memory, time, and structure rather than trying to hold everything in mind at once.

Alongside professional support, many adults find it helpful to:

  • use visible external reminders such as digital calendars with timed alerts, whiteboards, or single-place checklists
  • break large tasks into small, concrete first steps so starting feels less overwhelming
  • create designated "landing zones" near the front door or desk for keys, wallets, phones, and essentials
  • work with visual time cues such as timers or time-blocking rather than relying on internal time sense
  • reduce friction in daily routines by simplifying steps around mornings, meals, and bills
  • build planned transitions and recovery breaks between demanding work or social commitments
  • practise self-compassion when routines slip, focusing on resetting simply rather than starting from scratch

Strategies work best when adapted to your work environment, household routines, and personal preferences.

What Could Support Look Like?

Individualised Care for Adults

Because adult ADHD frequently overlaps with other life stressors or mental health concerns, care is tailored around a thorough understanding of your needs.

Comprehensive ADHD Assessment

A clinically informed assessment typically involves a detailed clinical interview, review of developmental and life history, standardised rating scales, and screening for co-occurring concerns, followed by clear feedback and practical recommendations.

Psychological Therapy

Evidence-based approaches, such as Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) adapted for adult ADHD, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), and skills-based coaching strategies, may help build executive functioning tools, emotional regulation, and self-understanding.

Relationship and Family Support

Where ADHD-related patterns affect partnership dynamics or parenting, couples or family-focused sessions can support clearer communication and practical shared routines.

GP and Medical Support

If you are considering a medical review or exploring broader healthcare options alongside psychological care, your General Practitioner (GP) can provide referrals to an appropriate psychiatrist or medical specialist for further medical assessment.

You Don't Need to Know Where to Start

Navigating Assessment and Therapy With Clarity

Knowing whether you need a diagnostic assessment, ongoing therapy, a GP referral, or a combination of supports can feel confusing, especially when executive functioning already feels stretched.

You do not need to have everything worked out before contacting us.

At Michelle Barratt Psychology, our team listens carefully to what you have been experiencing, explains our assessment and therapy pathways clearly, and helps connect you with an appropriate practitioner.

Whether you are:

  • exploring adult ADHD concerns for the first time
  • seeking a structured psychological assessment and report
  • looking for practical therapy strategies following a diagnosis
  • navigating co-occurring anxiety, burnout, or relationship stress
  • wanting in-person sessions in Brisbane or flexible online appointments

we are here to help make the process clearer and more manageable.

Why Clients Choose MBP

Clinically Informed Support, With You at the Centre

Michelle Barratt Psychology & Administration Services (MBP) provides a welcoming, neutral, and professionally managed entry point for adults seeking psychological assessment and therapy.

Clinically Informed Intake

Thoughtful intake processes help us understand your concerns and identify an appropriate assessment or therapy pathway.

Appropriate Practitioner Matching

We connect you with clinical psychologists, general psychologists, social workers, or counsellors whose scope of practice and experience align with adult ADHD care.

Structured Assessment & Reporting

Where clinical assessment is undertaken, practitioners provide clear, thorough feedback and tailored recommendations.

Coordinated Care

Where appropriate and with your consent, practitioners can liaise with your GP, psychiatrist, and other health professionals involved in your care.

Practical Referral Support

Our team assists with GP referral requirements, Mental Health Treatment Plans, and Medicare-related paperwork where applicable.

Flexible Access

In-person appointments are available at our Brisbane clinics in Toowong and Manly West, alongside secure Online Therapy / Telehealth Australia-wide where clinically appropriate.
